newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish Loyalists silent on truce pleas.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish Loyalists silent on truce pleas.

text.p: Outlawed Protestant gunmen kept a sinister silence on Saturday despite a flood of entreaties to keep alive a fragile two-year Northern Irish truce.
Fears of a breakdown in a Protestant Loyalist' ceasefire grew after their Catholic-supported IRA foes set off their first bombs for two years in the British-ruled province, killing a soldier.
Politicians linked to the guerrillas, called Loyalists because of their fervent allegiance to Britain, pleaded for the ceasefire to remain intact to avert a new cycle of sectarian warfare.

They echoed appeals by political leaders in Britain, Ireland and the United States, fearful of the collapse of a struggling three-year peace process and the nighmare prospect of rival guerrillas in open warfare once more.

Loyalist sources refused to speculate on the guerrilla commanders' decision and said they did not know whether a public statement would be issued on Sunday to coincide with the second anniversary of the their truce.
But the Belfast morning Irish News forecast "Loyalists to hold the line on ceasefire", quoting unidentified sources.

Loyalist politicians gave public warnings to the guerrilla groups' umbrella body, the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC), that abandonment of the truce would play into the hands of Irish Republican Army hawks wanting renewed all-out conflict.
"I make this appeal - stand firm," Hugh Smyth, leader of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP), political arm of the banned Ulster Volunteer Force, told his annual conference on Saturday.

"Don't give in now, we have come too far. Don't allow the Provos (IRA) to use the Loyalist paramilitaries as their way of getting off the hook - because at the moment that would mean a return to violence by Loyalist paramilitaries."
Other senior PUP figures implored the CLMC to to heed a widespread yearning for peace.

"It is important for the Loyalist paramilitaries to pay attention to what the people are saying...the people don't want a return to Loyalist violence," Gusty Spence, the acknowledged "elder statesman" of Loyalist politics, told Reuters.
"We have done all that we possibly can do in order to maintain the ceasefire, to tell the paramilitaries not to recommence violence," said Spence, 63, a former guerrilla who is now a PUP leader.
"The IRA (Irish Republican Army) have done all in their power to blow the Loyalist ceasefire sky high."
Spence was the man chosen by the CLMC to announce its historic truce to a euphoric Northern Ireland in 1994.

Loyalists had killed hundreds of Catholics in a battle to thwart the IRA's aim of breaking British rule and the twin ceasefires seemed to signal a fresh start after a 25-year war which claimed 3,200 lives.

The IRA resumed hostilies last February, with the first of a string of bombs in London. Last Monday they detonated two car bombs inside British military headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast, killing a senior non-commissioned officer.
